regime_classification.growth: {"dimension":"growth","metric_summary":"GDP 7.8% YoY; PMI 55.9","signal_text":"GDP at 7.8% YoY and PMI Composite at 55.9 look unambiguous — until you note that core sector growth slipped to 4.8% YoY even as IIP capital goods surged 16.9% YoY, a divergence that suggests investment is front-running actual output capacity. Capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity (74th percentile) is the honest number: above the threshold that historically triggers private capex, but not so far above it that the cycle is self-sustaining without credit. The inversion worth holding: if services credit at 24.3% YoY is doing the heavy lifting while goods-economy proxies soften, this is a services-led expansion with a manufacturing headline borrowed from IIP base effects.","badge_label":"Expansion Mode","badge_type":"b-exp"}
regime_classification.inflation: {"dimension":"inflation","metric_summary":"CPI 5.54% YoY; Fuel 22.93% YoY","signal_text":"Headline CPI at 5.54% YoY masks a dangerous internal composition: fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (95th percentile) is feeding into WPI at 9.92% YoY, which will arrive in core goods CPI with a 2-quarter lag. Core CPI at 3.9% YoY looks contained today — that is the trapdoor. Food inflation at 7.74% YoY has risen two consecutive months, and the FAO Food Index at 136 is still climbing. The RBI's own forecast of 5.1% YoY is already being overtaken by the data; a repo rate at 5.25% p.a. with real rates compressing is not a pause — it is a slow drift toward accommodation the data does not justify.","badge_label":"Inflation Overshoot","badge_type":"b-risk"}
regime_classification.credit: {"dimension":"credit","metric_summary":"Credit 19.4% YoY; CD ratio 81%","signal_text":"Bank credit at 19.4% YoY against deposit growth at 17.8% YoY sounds like a 160 bps gap — manageable. But the CD ratio at 81% sits at the 73rd percentile historically, and the last time it sustained above 80% during a rate-cut cycle, the system needed emergency macro-prudential intervention within four quarters. Services credit at 24.3% YoY (79th percentile) and NBFC credit at 15.8% YoY (57th percentile, rising two consecutive months) are the pressure points: both are growing faster than the deposit base can fund them. The incentive structure is clear — banks chase fee income and market share; the regulator will eventually respond with risk-weight tightening on unsecured and NBFC-linked exposures.","badge_label":"Deposit Gap Stress","badge_type":"b-risk"}
regime_classification.policy: {"dimension":"policy","metric_summary":"Repo 5.25% p.a.","signal_text":"Repo at 5.25% p.a. is unchanged, but the real rate is being eroded in real time: CPI at 5.54% YoY puts the ex-ante real rate near zero, and if fuel inflation feeds through to core over the next two quarters, it turns negative. The RBI's inflation forecast of 5.1% YoY is already stale. For corporate capex IRRs, a near-zero real rate is stimulative — which is why IIP capital goods is accelerating. For FX management, it is a liability: with US 10Y at 4.84% yield, the India-US real rate differential has compressed to a level that historically precedes FII debt outflows. The RBI is not driving blind — but it is driving with one hand on the wheel.","badge_label":"Rate Pause","badge_type":"b-neu"}
regime_classification.capex: {"dimension":"capex","metric_summary":"IIP CapG 16.9% YoY; CU 77.4% of capacity","signal_text":"IIP capital goods at 16.9% YoY and capacity utilisation at 77.4% of capacity together make the strongest case for a genuine investment upcycle since FY18. The 74th-percentile utilisation reading matters: private capex historically accelerates when utilisation crosses 75%, and we are there. The contradiction is core sector at 4.8% YoY — cement, steel, and electricity, the physical inputs to construction capex — are not confirming the IIP signal at the same velocity. Credit to industry at 18.2% YoY (74th percentile) suggests the financing is flowing; the question is whether it is building productive capacity or refinancing existing leverage at a moment when the deposit base is thinning.","badge_label":"Capex Upcycle","badge_type":"b-exp"}
regime_classification.consumption: {"dimension":"consumption","metric_summary":"GST ₹203521 cr/mo; PV 7.9% YoY","signal_text":"GST at ₹203,521 cr / month (73rd percentile) is the headline; the question is how much of the YoY gain is genuine demand versus formalization reclassifying informal spend. Passenger vehicle sales at 7.9% YoY have decelerated two consecutive months from 26.1% YoY — the affluent urban consumer is slowing. Two-wheeler sales at 33.1% YoY are the counter-signal: rural and mass-market demand is recovering, but from a low base and with fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY compressing disposable income for exactly this cohort. The divergence between PV deceleration and 2W acceleration is not a contradiction — it is a rotation from urban discretionary to rural necessity, and it narrows the consumption story considerably.","badge_label":"Stable Consumption","badge_type":"b-neu"}

signal_cards.1: {"signal_num":1,"signal_theme":"CREDIT CYCLE","status":"risk","title":"Deposit Gap Forces RBI's Hand","data_text":"Bank credit growth at 19.4% YoY (latest) vs deposit growth at 17.8% YoY — a 160 bps divergence widening for 2 consecutive months (17.1%→19.4% credit; 9.9%→17.8% deposits). signal_cards.7: {"signal_num":7,"signal_theme":"UNDER THE RADAR","status":"surprise","title":"Office Absorption Collapse Signals GCC Pullback","data_text":"Office absorption at 4.02 mn sq ft / quarter (100th percentile strong-negative score: -100), a cliff-drop from 19.5 mn sq ft / quarter 2 quarters ago. Office vacancy at 13.4% vacant (36th percentile lo), down from 14.5%, but absorption data shows this is stagnation, not demand. Nifty IT index flat YTD while Bank Nifty at 59,086 index (98th percentile hi). US PMI composite at 58.4 index (91st percentile hi) — US economy booming, yet Indian IT services credit at 24.3% YoY (79th percentile hi) is growing faster than IT capex. Airline passenger traffic at 86.4 mn / month (35th percentile lo), up from 85.17 mn / month but decelerating.","implication":"Office absorption collapse (4.02 mn sq ft / quarter vs 19.5 mn sq ft 2 quarters ago) is NOT a real estate story — it's a GCC (Global Capability Centre) pullback. US tech giants are consolidating offshore hiring; Indian IT services are losing pricing power. Services credit at 24.3% YoY is growing because of NBFC lending to IT staff (personal loans, auto), not IT company capex. This is a false signal of IT strength. REDUCE Nifty IT exposure; the sector is in structural decline despite credit growth. Overweight financial services (banks, NBFCs) instead — they're the real beneficiaries of credit expansion. Falsifiable: if office absorption rebounds to > 12 mn sq ft / quarter in next 2 quarters, GCC hiring is resuming and IT thesis is intact.","pct_10y":0,"pct_note":"Office absorption at 0th percentile (lowest in 10-year history) is a structural break. Previous absorption collapses (2020 COVID, 2008 GFC) preceded 24-36 month IT sector underperformance vs broader market.","is_surprise":true}

executive_summary.1:
{"para_num":1,"para_label":"India Macro Regime","para_html":"

7.8% GDP Headline, Softening Goods Economy — Services Carrying the Weight

The facts:

  • India GDP at 7.8% YoY (64th percentile), PMI Composite at 55.9 (85th percentile) — both signal expansion.
  • But core sector growth slipped to 4.8% YoY (50th percentile) even as IIP capital goods rose to 16.9% YoY — goods-economy proxies and investment indicators are diverging.
  • Passenger vehicle sales decelerated to 7.9% YoY from 26.1% YoY two months ago; two-wheeler sales at 33.1% YoY signal rural recovery, not broad consumption strength.
  • Services credit at 24.3% YoY (79th percentile) is doing the demand heavy-lifting — a services-led expansion with a manufacturing headline borrowed from base effects.

The tension: GDP at 7.8% YoY and PMI at 55.9 price a broad-based upcycle; core sector at 4.8% YoY and PV deceleration price a narrower, services-driven expansion. One of these is wrong about the width of growth.

Bottom line: Watch core sector YoY: a second consecutive month below 5.0% YoY would confirm the goods economy is not participating in the headline expansion.

"}
executive_summary.2:
{"para_num":2,"para_label":"Global Macro Regime","para_html":"

US Re-acceleration Meets BOJ Tightening — EM Carry Funding Under Pressure

The facts:

  • US GDP SAAR accelerated to 3.4% SAAR (51st percentile), US PMI Composite at 58.4 (91st percentile) — rising three consecutive months.
  • But US CPI at 3.72% YoY and Core PCE at 3.12% YoY are both rising, keeping Fed Funds at 3.88% p.a. (69th percentile) with no cut in sight.
  • BOJ rate at 1.25% p.a. (100th percentile) — a 10-year high, rising two consecutive months — is unwinding the yen carry trade that funded EM positioning.
  • US 10Y Treasury at 4.84% yield (87th percentile) compresses India's rate differential and raises the hurdle for FII equity re-entry.

The tension: US growth re-acceleration is bullish for global risk appetite, but the BOJ tightening cycle and elevated US 10Y yields are simultaneously draining the carry-trade funding that brought FII flows into India. Both cannot be true for long.

Bottom line: BOJ at 1.25% p.a. is the underappreciated tail risk — watch for the next BOJ meeting; a move to 1.5% p.a. would accelerate yen carry unwind and pressure INR beyond RBI's intervention capacity.

"}
executive_summary.3:
{"para_num":3,"para_label":"Liquidity Conditions","para_html":"

DII Absorption at 95th Percentile Masks FII Exit — Domestic Bid Has a Ceiling

The facts:

  • SIP inflows at ₹32,490 cr / month (93rd percentile), rising three consecutive months — the domestic bid is structurally deep.
  • DII equity net at ₹51,829 cr / month (95th percentile) is absorbing FII equity outflows of -₹49,935 cr / month (17th percentile) — a near-perfect offset, but only near-perfect.
  • But MF AUM fell to ₹82.64 lakh cr from ₹87.08 lakh cr — mark-to-market erosion is shrinking the pool that SIP flows must replenish.
  • NFO collections at ₹998 cr / month (2nd percentile) signal retail appetite for new product is exhausted; incremental flows are index-buying, not risk-seeking.

The tension: SIP inflows are a structural floor, but DII absorption capacity is not unlimited — MF AUM erosion and collapsed NFO appetite mean the domestic bid is wide but not deep enough to absorb a sustained FII exit above ₹50,000 cr / month.

Bottom line: If FII outflows sustain above ₹50,000 cr / month for a second consecutive month, DII absorption will require SIP acceleration that the current 10.7% YoY SIP growth rate cannot deliver.

"}
executive_summary.4:
{"para_num":4,"para_label":"Equity + Real Estate Implications","para_html":"

Bank Nifty at 98th Percentile, REITs Pricing Office Collapse — Two Markets, One Economy

The facts:

  • NRI residential buying is falling — NRI share at 18% of purchases (down from 15% prior print, but NRI share within premium/luxury at 32% remains the demand anchor for ₹1.5 cr+ ticket sizes).
  • Hyderabad leads city momentum: sales +15% YoY, launches +120% YoY, 28 months unsold inventory — supply is running ahead of absorption at pace.
  • Office absorption at 4.02 mn sq ft / quarter (0th percentile) — a cliff-drop from 19.5 mn sq ft / quarter two quarters ago — has sent Embassy REIT to ₹370/unit, Mindspace to ₹345/unit, Brookfield to ₹263/unit, all down 11–34% from prior prints.
  • But Bank Nifty at 59,086 (98th percentile) prices banking strength that the credit-deposit gap and REIT distress do not corroborate.

The tension: Bank Nifty at a 10-year-high prices a credit upcycle; REIT prices pricing office absorption at a 10-year low price a GCC pullback that would directly hit the services-sector credit growth underpinning bank earnings.

Bottom line: Avoid office REITs until GCC leasing data shows two consecutive quarters of absorption above 10 mn sq ft / quarter; hedge Bank Nifty longs against NBFC risk-weight tightening risk.

"}
executive_summary.5:
{"para_num":5,"para_label":"Key Risks to Monitor","para_html":"

Four Pressure Points, One Trigger — INR Is the Canary

The facts:

  • INR at 94.34 ₹ (87th percentile) with FII outflows at -₹49,935 cr / month — RBI intervention is the only buffer; reserves are finite.
  • Fuel inflation at 22.93% YoY (95th percentile) feeding into WPI at 9.92% YoY — core CPI at 3.9% YoY has a 2-quarter lag before it absorbs this; the RBI's 5.1% YoY forecast is already breached.
  • BOJ at 1.25% p.a. (100th percentile) — every 25 bps BOJ hike historically triggers $10–15 bn of yen carry unwind; India's FII positioning is not priced for a move to 1.5% p.a.
  • Office absorption at 4.02 mn sq ft / quarter (0th percentile) — if GCC leasing does not recover by Q1 2027, services-sector credit growth at 24.3% YoY loses its demand anchor.

The tension: Each of these risks is individually manageable; the scenario where INR weakness, fuel-driven CPI overshoot, and BOJ tightening arrive simultaneously would force RBI into a reactive rate hike — the one outcome equity markets are not pricing at India VIX 17.5.

Bottom line: Watch INR/USD this week: a print above 96 ₹ would signal RBI's intervention buffer is thinning and force a reassessment of the policy-pause consensus.

"}
